chunks.content: Unless you’re living underground, you’ve probably met or heard of someone talking about buying or selling a small business. The Silver Tsunami Is Here – and It’s Not Slowing Down First, the obvious demographic megatrend: the Silver Tsunami. This term refers to the massive wave of Baby Boomer business owners heading into retirement. According to the U.S. Census Bureau, roughly 10,000 Baby Boomers turn 65 every single day, and this will continue into the 2030s. A recent study from BizBuySell notes that retirement is the #1 reason for selling a small business, cited in nearly 60% of listings But what’s surprising is that this isn’t limited to those over 70. In today’s cultural climate, retirement doesn’t start at 65—it starts when people feel like they’ve had enough. Many business owners in their mid-50s to early 60s are increasingly opting for early exits, seeking more time for family, health, or passion projects, rather than clinging to the old “work-until-you-drop” model. As CNBC reported in 2023, early retirement among 55–64-year-olds rose significantly post-pandemic, accelerating transitions that once took decades. Now, younger generations are reaching retirement at the same time as their parents, leaving the older professionals—who once hoped to pass the torch to slightly younger colleagues—stranded without successors. That’s millions of businesses quietly coming up for sale—not only because owners are aging, but because they’re done playing by outdated rules. Millennials and Gen Xers Want Lifestyle and Autonomy—Not Corner Offices On the other side of the coin, you’ve got a rising generation of buyers—many in their 30s and 40s—who grew up reading The 4-Hour Workweek, watching startup culture blossom (and in many cases, crash), and dreaming not of traditional employment, but of freedom. These folks don’t want to reinvent the wheel—they want a profitable lifestyle business they can grow, modernize, and run from a laptop in Tulum if they feel like it. BOX- Millennials and Gen Xers came of age during the “work optional” era, and while few want to fully retire at 35, most are chasing autonomy and purpose over cubicles and their position in an chart. Buying an established business fits perfectly into that vision: it’s a faster, smarter way to build wealth without the chaos and high failure rate of starting from scratch. The people in this age group were raised with the expectation of climbing the corporate ladder, getting degrees, and “working hard” in traditional careers... but by the time they graduated, the landscape had shifted. They experienced The rise of the internet, The collapse of job security, The 2008 financial crisis, Dot-com bubble On top of this, at this point in their mid-life careers, they’ve ridden the waves of the birth of remote work and online entrepreneurship; and The COVID pandemic and return-to-work. Back The 4-Hour Workweek came out in 2007, it felt like someone had finally given language to what they were already craving: freedom, flexibility, and the ability to design a life, not a career. It wasn’t a productivity book—it was a manifesto for a generation watching the old playbook fall apart. Ferriss introduced ideas like “mini-retirements,” lifestyle arbitrage, and building systems that free you from time-for-money traps. For many in this age group—especially professionals disillusioned with corporate burnout or traditional service firms—it wasn’t inspiring. It was permission to leave the grind behind. --- It’s worth noting: 20% of small business buyers today are under 40, up from 10% a decade ago The Startup Bubble Has Popped—And That’s a Good Thing Let’s talk tech. The early 2010s were a gold rush of innovation—Airbnb, Uber, Instagram—but the era of “let’s disrupt everything” has fizzled. Most of the low-hanging fruit has already been picked or failed. Investors know it. Founders know it. Venture apitalists know it. And wannabe entrepreneurs are realizing that starting a business from scratch means massive burn rates, years of hustle, and no guarantee of profit. I represented startups as a lawyer for years. I had a front row seat to how the tech startup dream captivated a generation. Fueled by headlines about Facebook, Uber, Airbnb, and a handful of Silicon Valley unicorns, it painted a picture of meteoric success: a scrappy founder with a big idea, a hoodie, and a laptop changes the world—and cashes out for billions. But that dream? For most, it was a mirage. The startup world runs on a gambler’s logic. Venture capitalists fund dozens—sometimes hundreds—of early-stage companies not because they expect most to succeed, but because they don’t have to. They’re playing a portfolio game. If one in twenty hits big, the fund wins. It's a game of asymmetrical returns, where the backers hedge their bets with volume. But the founders? They don’t get to diversify. For them, success is binary: they either make it, or they don’t. And unlike in poker, being close doesn’t count.

Fueled by headlines about Facebook, Uber, Airbnb, and a handful of Silicon Valley unicorns, it painted a picture of meteoric success: a scrappy founder with a big idea, a hoodie, and a laptop changes the world—and cashes out for billions. But that dream? For most, it was a mirage. The startup world runs on a gambler’s logic. Venture capitalists fund dozens—sometimes hundreds—of early-stage companies not because they expect most to succeed, but because they don’t have to. They’re playing a portfolio game. If one in twenty hits big, the fund wins. It's a game of asymmetrical returns, where the backers hedge their bets with volume. But the founders? They don’t get to diversify. For them, success is binary: they either make it, or they don’t. And unlike in poker, being close doesn’t count. You can build a great product, a strong team, even reach revenue—and walk away with nothing if you don’t make it to a liquidity event. Or if you do... it may not be what you expected. Because here’s the part the media rarely covers that I saw happen over and over again: even in the rare cases where a startup "wins," founders often find themselves diluted down through successive rounds of fundraising—Series A, B, C, D—until their equity is a sliver of what it was. Add in complex preferred return waterfalls—which prioritize investors recouping 1x, 2x, or more before common shareholders see a dime—and it’s no surprise that some founders walk away from their own “success” with little more than a press release and a burnout badge. I can’t tell you how many times I saw the inside workings of a deal that was little more than a bankruptcy only to see it covered in the media as an enviable “Merger” or other success story. The startup myth persists because it's emotionally intoxicating. It appeals to youthful optimism, rebellious spirit, and the idea that you can skip the line. But the reality is that for most founders, especially first-time entrepreneurs, the odds are long, the path is brutal, and the outcome is rarely what it seems. Professionals in their mid-30s and early 40s have weathered enough volatility—from recessions to a global pandemic—that they tend to favor more stable, conservative paths forward. Startup Failure Rates: Approximately 90% of startups fail, with about 10% shutting down within their first year. General Business Failure Rates: In contrast, about 23.2% of private sector businesses in the U.S. fail within their first year. Factors Contributing to the Stability of Existing Businesses: Established Market Presence: Existing businesses have a proven track record, established customer base, and recognized brand, reducing the uncertainty associated with market entry. Operational Experience: They possess refined operational processes and experienced staff, leading to more predictable and efficient operations. Financial History: Access to historical financial data allows for better forecasting and financial planning, making it easier to secure financing if needed. Searchfunds and Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition Enter the Scene According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, only about 50% of startups survive five years, and 1 in 10 becomes “high-growth.” Compare that to buying a business that’s already profitable, already has customers, and can be financed with leverage. It’s no wonder searchfunds and acquisition entrepreneurship are having a major moment. 1. Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition (ETA) Is a Growing Movement More and more business school grads are skipping the startup scene and heading straight into acquiring existing businesses. Stanford, Harvard, Wharton, Booth, and INSEAD all now offer ETA-focused programs and clubs. Stanford’s Search Fund Primer and biennial study are among the most accessed entrepreneurial resources from its Graduate School of Business. This isn’t academic theory—it’s a cultural shift. The idea of buying a “boring” but profitable business is increasingly appealing to those who want control, cash flow, and freedom—without have to live on a friend’s couch for years to get there. 2. Investor Attention Has Shifted Family offices and micro-private equity firms have flooded the small business acquisition space. Instead of writing big checks for risky tech startups, they’re backing searchers acquiring $1M–$5M EBITDA businesses in home services, healthcare, bookkeeping, and B2B niches. It’s a lower-risk, cash-flow-heavy model with tangible assets and recession resilience. Platforms like: Searchfunder.com MicroAcquire (now Acquire.com) BizBuySell SMB Twitter / LinkedIn communities ...have exploded in usage, reflecting a booming interest in deal flow from both buyers and investors. Add to this, n recent years, there's been a significant shift in where private equity firms are placing their bets. Once enthralled with high-growth startups promising the next big disruption, private equity is now increasingly turning its attention to smaller, more stable, and often less glamorous businesses— including professional service firms like law offices, advisory businesses, and consulting practices.

It’s a lower-risk, cash-flow-heavy model with tangible assets and recession resilience. Platforms like: Searchfunder.com MicroAcquire (now Acquire.com) BizBuySell SMB Twitter / LinkedIn communities ...have exploded in usage, reflecting a booming interest in deal flow from both buyers and investors. Add to this, n recent years, there's been a significant shift in where private equity firms are placing their bets. Once enthralled with high-growth startups promising the next big disruption, private equity is now increasingly turning its attention to smaller, more stable, and often less glamorous businesses— including professional service firms like law offices, advisory businesses, and consulting practices. Why the pivot? The volatile climate in the startup world has pushed investors to seek safer returns. As Bloomberg reported in late 2023, many venture-backed startups began missing growth targets, burning cash at unsustainable rates, and facing down rounds or outright collapse. In contrast, small, profitable businesses with recurring revenue—like accounting firms—offered something venture capital didn’t: predictability and immediate cash flow. According to The Wall Street Journal, private equity firms have dramatically increased their acquisition of "mom-and-pop" businesses, citing the rise of what's called the “Silver Tsunami” of retiring baby boomers who own successful local businesses but lack clear succession plans. These acquisitions now include dental offices, HVAC companies, and yes—accounting practices. It's part of a trend that The Journal dubbed “The Big Buy-Up of Small Biz.” Backing this up, Stanford’s 2024 Search Fund Study noted a record number of new search funds launched in 2023 and the median deal size shrank to $14.4 million, reflecting a growing appetite for smaller firms with stable earnings. This coincides with private equity and independent searchers swarming the lower middle market—a segment once overlooked but now red hot. As Axios recently reported, “Private equity firms are acting more like small business buyers than big corporate raiders,” with portfolio diversification now leaning heavily toward fragmented industries. This also aligns with an emerging focus on industries that offer services people can’t live without—like tax prep, bookkeeping, and compliance—which remain recession-resistant and ripe for optimization. In short, private equity has left Silicon Valley behind for Main Street America. And for business owners eyeing succession or sale, this shift presents a golden opportunity—one where financial and strategic buyers are increasingly eager to write checks for steady businesses with clean books, recurring revenue, and owner-operators ready to retire. Walker Deibel’s book Buy Then Build launched in 2018, and it was a watershed moment. It made this path not only accessible but desirable. Around the same time, Harvard Business School released its HBR Guide to Buying a Small Business in 2017, distilling its long-standing ETA (Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition) course into a book for the rest of us. The search fund model—first coined in 1984—has officially gone mainstream. Interest Rates, Real Estate, and Crypto: The Investment Landscape Has Shifted Coming from the other angle of traditional non-startup investment, Maintreet businesses are also attracting interest. Let’s not forget the elephant in the room: traditional investment strategies don’t look as shiny anymore. Real estate? With current higher interest rates, most deals simply don’t pencil anymore unless you’re all cash or highly leveraged. Stocks? Predictable but uninspiring. Crypto? What once felt like financial utopia is now under regulatory scrutiny and trades basically in lockstep with the S&P 500. And now, layer on top of all this a wave of political and global uncertainty. Election cycles, geopolitical tension, regulatory shifts—these aren’t background noise anymore. They’re front-and-center drivers of market volatility. Investors are realizing that even “safe” investments aren’t immune to sudden shocks. When you’re constantly wondering how the next policy announcement or international headline will impact your portfolio, it’s no wonder people are looking for something more tangible. That’s where Main Street comes in. Buying a small business—especially one with recurring revenue, stable clients, and a solid local presence—starts to feel less like a risky bet and more like a strategic hedge. You’re not buying into revenue; you’re buying into control, consistency, and community. Enter small business acquisition—one of the last frontiers where you can find leverageable deals, direct control, and serious cash flow. With SBA 7(a) loans, buyers can finance up to 90% or more of a business with as little as 10% down. Even better, the business itself acts as collateral—not your house or your savings. These loans were originally designed to help entrepreneurs access capital and now, more than ever, they’re being used to buy existing cash-flowing businesses, not start new ones. In fact, the SBA reported over $27 billion in 7(a) loans in 2023, with a large and growing portion being used for business acquisitions The COVID Wake-Up Call—and the Remote Work Revolution Then came COVID.

Nearly 40 million Americans lost jobs in the early months of the pandemic, and for many, it shattered the illusion of security in traditional employment. Even those who returned to work didn’t return with the same mindset. The “Great Resignation” of 2021 reflected a massive psychological shift. People didn’t want to change jobs; they wanted to change their lives. They wanted more flexibility, more meaning, and more control. That mindset didn’t go away. Today, many mid-career professionals are seeking remote-first, lifestyle-friendly options. Owning a service-based business—or acquiring one with an already remote team—has become one of the most attractive paths forward.
